analysis.one_liner: Creates an independent board to police auditors and bans accounting firms from consulting for the companies they audit.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or vote, and the 107th Congress ended in January 2003 with it never brought to the floor.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Enron collapse exposed that accounting firms were auditing the same companies they also consulted for, Senator Dodd proposed a bill to tighten the rules. It would create an independent board, overseen by the SEC, to register accounting firms, inspect their work, and discipline them; ban auditors from selling consulting services to the companies they audit; block the revolving door between audit firms and their clients; and add 150 accountants to the SEC's staff. The bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who own stock directly or through retirement and mutual funds would gain a check on the accounting firms whose clean audit opinions had vouched for collapsed companies. The bill would let an independent board inspect audit firms, discipline them, and fine them up to $15 million for fraud-related violations; it would ban auditors from selling consulting services to their own audit clients; and it would bar companies from hiring as financial officers people who had worked at their audit firm within the past two years [S2] [S3]. It would also add 150 accounting professionals to the SEC's oversight staff [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirement savers and everyday stock investors

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Independent Public Accounting Board, overseen by the SEC but funded by fees on the firms themselves, to register all firms that audit public companies, inspect their work annually or every two years, and discipline violators with fines, suspension, or revocation

Bans auditors from selling bookkeeping, IT consulting, valuation, internal-audit outsourcing, legal, and most other non-audit services to a company at the same time they audit it, addressing the conflict in which firms vetted their own consulting work

Prohibits a firm from auditing a company whose comptroller, chief accounting officer, or chief financial officer worked at that firm in the previous two years, cutting the revolving door between auditors and client management

Makes it unlawful for corporate officers or directors to mislead or pressure their own auditors, and requires prompt electronic disclosure of insider transactions and of dealings with affiliates and off-balance-sheet entities
Adds 150 qualified accounting professionals to the SEC to strengthen oversight of auditors, and directs the SEC to recommend stricter accounting rules for stock options and special purpose entities

analysis.who_pays: Large public accounting firms would bear most of the cost: they would lose the ability to sell consulting, IT, legal, and other non-audit services to companies they audit, pay registration and annual fees to fund the new regulator, and face fines up to $2 million per violation ($15 million for fraud) [S3]. Publicly traded companies would pay more for audits and face new disclosure requirements for deals with affiliates and off-balance-sheet entities [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Large accounting firms and public companies

drawbacks.text: The bill would let the SEC exempt any accounting firm, audit report, or class of firms from any provision of the act if it finds the exemption consistent with the public interest, a broad waiver that could hollow out the rules in practice

The new regulator would be a private entity rather than a government agency, and its members would be chosen largely by the Federal Reserve chair, the Treasury Secretary, and the SEC chair, raising questions about democratic accountability

Banning auditors from providing most non-audit services would cut off revenue that large firms and their clients had built into their relationships, raising compliance and audit costs for public companies — costs that can be passed to shareholders
The bill only studied, rather than adopted, mandatory rotation of audit firms, leaving the central question of auditor dependence on large clients unresolved

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is a direct response to a real, documented failure: audit firms policing the companies that paid them for lucrative consulting work. The restrictions on non-audit services and the revolving door target exactly the conflicts that let bad audits stand, and the costs fall mainly on the firms and companies that created the problem. The design is not perfect — the SEC waiver authority is broad, the regulator would be private rather than governmental, and the biggest question, mandatory auditor rotation, is punted to a study. But on balance this is a substantial investor-protection bill whose burdens fall on concentrated interests.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and sat there with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dodd introduced the bill on March 8, 2002, during the wave of corporate accounting scandals, and four Democratic senators joined as cosponsors
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, where no further recorded action was ever taken
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 with the bill still in committee, never having received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote

The bill's core ideas — an independent auditor regulator, bans on non-audit services for audit clients, and a two-year cooling-off period for auditors who join client companies — appeared later that year in the accounting overhaul that did become law

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large accounting firms and their corporate clients kept the existing arrangement, in which firms could audit a company while selling it consulting services, through the remainder of the 107th Congress. Comparable investor protections became law later in 2002 through separate legislation, so the public's loss from this bill's death was temporary.

sides.party_line_note: Only five senators, all Democrats, are on record supporting the bill; no Republican took a position on the record before it died in committee.

industries.industry: Public accounting firms (the large audit firms)
industries.note: The bill would ban these firms from selling consulting, IT, legal, and other non-audit services to companies they audit, ending a practice in which firms earned more from a client's consulting than from its audit. It would also require registration, regular inspections, and fees to fund a new regulator with the power to fine them.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their executives
industries.note: Executives would face new criminal exposure for misleading their own auditors, companies would have to disclose transactions with affiliates and off-balance-sheet entities promptly and in electronic form, and the SEC would be directed to push for stricter treatment of stock options and special purpose entities.
The bill would mandate at least 150 additional accounting professionals at the SEC to review audit firms and discipline bad audits, with funding authorized separately from the agency's normal budget.
